The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00234

Whenever the movement for the descendants of Ali is mentioned, so too are the study of ideas, the schools of philosophy, wisdom and Sufism, and every form of inquiry that challenges what is openly visible and gives weight to what lies hidden beneath it. The supporters of Ali's family favoured change precisely because they opposed the ruling power and the existing order. Philosophy in its many branches had become intertwined with politics, especially with questions of the caliphate, kingship and religious leadership. The rightful imam was now one thing, and the ruler who had usurped power quite another.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00235

Persian influence can be seen in the Shia idea of wasiyya, the designation of a successor. The imam whom the movement supported would name his successor before his death and inform his leading organisers to avoid divisions. Since Islam calls for consultation in choosing the imam, we must trace this idea of appointment to Persian traditions of government. There, kingship had been the exclusive preserve of the Sasanian royal family, passed down from generation to generation.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00236

There is also the idea of the awaited Mahdi: the imam who has gone into hiding until he returns at the right moment to fill the earth with justice after it has been filled with oppression and wrongdoing. This idea tells us a great deal about the Shia movement's new approach. It expressed a continuing hope of liberation, despite the harsh conditions that forced the imam into hiding. His disappearance was known as the ghayba (absence); the period of waiting for him as tawaqquf (suspension of judgement); and his reappearance as the raj'a (return). The Persian imagination played a large part in shaping these and other beliefs.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00237

Likewise, the principle of unquestioning obedience to the imams — one of the chief foundations of successful underground work — found its way into Shia political beliefs through Persian tradition, in which obedience to the Persian kings was regarded as a sacred duty.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00238

The belief in hidden meanings, known as ta'wil batini, held that things have both an outward and an inner meaning. It entered Shia political thought from Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism. Clearly, the Shia movement drew on this belief when interpreting the Quran and the Prophet's teachings in ways that supported the claim of Ali's family to leadership.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00239

But the Shia belief that most clearly justified underground activity was taqiyya: concealing one's true beliefs in the face of danger. It also underlined the importance of discretion and secrecy in supporting an imam who remained hidden, through loyal organisers who obtained secret pledges of allegiance on his behalf from followers and supporters. When conditions were favourable, the revolution would break out, and upon its success its champion, the awaited Mahdi, would appear.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00240

In short, the Shia movement's turn to underground activity grew out of the intellectual, religious, economic and social conditions of its time. Ultimately, it was born of bitter suffering and harsh persecution, which drove the oppressed to adopt this approach against a formidable enemy. The organised underground movement of the Shia began after Husayn's martyrdom and reached its height under Abu Hashim ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya. What we need to explain now is how and why the Abbasids took the movement for themselves, assumed control of its carefully built organisation and denied its true pioneers the fruits of their labour.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00241

It is generally accepted that the Abbasids, descended from al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's uncle (peace and blessings be upon him), played no leading role in the dispute over the imamate that gave rise to the political parties. Al-Abbas could not have claimed the caliphate after the Prophet's death, since he had embraced Islam relatively late. The accounts say that he offered to pledge allegiance to his nephew Ali as caliph. But for reasons we need not go into here, the caliphate passed to Abu Bakr, then to Umar, and then to Uthman.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00242

When Ali became caliph after Uthman's murder, his cousins Abd Allah and Ubayd Allah, the sons of al-Abbas, supported him. Ali made the first governor of Basra and the second governor of Yemen. But when Ali's fortunes declined after the arbitration, his cousins deserted him and sided with his rival Muawiya. Power settled in the hands of the Umayyad family. The descendants of Ali launched unsuccessful revolts and, as we have seen, turned to organised underground activity.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00243

The Abbasids then sought to join the movement of Ali's descendants. Ali ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Abbas cultivated a close relationship with Abu Hashim ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, the imam of the time whom the organisers supported. He lived with him in the village of Humayma, the centre of the movement. When Abu Hashim felt his death approaching, he had to choose a successor. Not one man of Ali's family was left who could take on the responsibility: the swords of the Umayyads had cut down their young men. Abu Hashim saw no alternative but to entrust the task to Ali ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Abbas. He made him his designated successor, let him into the movement's secrets, told him who its organisers were and gave him the written instructions of succession to present to them after his death. Abu Hashim died in 100 AH. Ali took up the task and became the imam of the time. The young men of Ali's family acknowledged his leadership until they were strong enough to resume their place at the head of the movement.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00244

The organisers accepted his leadership because he belonged to the Prophet's family. They made no distinction at the time between a leader from Ali's family and one from the Abbasid family, provided the cause remained in the Prophet's lineage. The masses of mawali cared little about the identity of the imam. What mattered much more to them was whether the movement achieved its aims. They were ready to support any imam who could free them from the grip of Umayyad rule. This helps explain how little questions of doctrine mattered compared with the social forces driving the movement. Nor did an Abbasid assuming its leadership mean giving up hope that the descendants of Ali might one day lead it again. It is certain that most of them turned their attention to scholarship and devoted themselves to learning. The trials and atrocities they had suffered had left them with little appetite for political activity. Divisions within their own family also helped the Abbasids remain at the head of the underground movement.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00245

The Abbasids proved remarkably effective at running the movement. They showed a rare gift for organisation, and the Ismailis and Qarmatians would later follow in their footsteps. They had made up their minds to take charge, but they kept their intentions to themselves. Had they made them public, the family of Ali and its loyal organisers would have turned against them, as would the masses who held the children of Ali and Fatima in such high regard.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00246

So the Abbasids came up with a clever slogan that would spare them an open dispute by deliberately blurring the issue. They called for “an acceptable leader from the family of Muhammad”. The slogan was vague enough to give them a claim to the leadership without provoking the problems that would have arisen had they openly promoted their own branch of the family alone.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00247

Their brilliance can also be seen in the attractive slogans they devised to speak to the hopes and aspirations of ordinary people. Take their call for equality. Equality is a fundamental principle of Islamic law, rooted in the Quran and the teachings of the Prophet. But as a political slogan, it was broad and undefined, leaving the Abbasids free to interpret it later as they saw fit. Nevertheless, the call for equality won over religious scholars and men of religion, who blessed the movement and joined it. It also drew in Arabs who had suffered as a result of the conflict between the Qays and Yemeni tribes. And after all the ethnic discrimination the mawali had endured under the Umayyads, the promise of equality was bound to draw them to the cause in great numbers. In short, everyone who resented Umayyad policy came together under the banner of equality. This testifies to the Abbasids' remarkable gift for building a movement and organising it.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00248

They also raised the banner of reform. Here was another attractive slogan that exposed the evils of Umayyad rule. It would allow the Abbasids, should they come to power, to claim the right to sweep away the old institutions and replace them with new ones within the bounds of Islamic law.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00249

The Abbasids' decision to concentrate their efforts on Khurasan showed judgement and foresight. Its people were renowned for their strength and courage, and they had remained relatively untouched by the political disputes and religious rivalries that had taken hold at the heart of the state. Ali ibn Abd Allah, the imam of the time, told his organisers:
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00251

... Seek out the people of Khurasan. They are many in number and clearly a hardy people. Their minds are unclouded and their hearts are open, not divided by rival passions or torn apart by deceit. ... I look with hope to the East, to the place where the lamp of the world and the light of creation rise.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00252

Those last words bring us to something on which the Abbasids placed great importance, and which was one of the main reasons their movement spread so widely: prophecy. Prophecies gave people hope, encouraged them to look forward to a new age and led them to believe that they were the soldiers and strength of the revolution, chosen by God to bring it about and help it triumph. The Abbasids spread the prophecies that circulated in their age and turned them to their own political ends. This shows their extraordinary talent for building and organising the movement.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00253

Belief in prophecies has been widespread in East and West alike. It is not a peculiarity of the Eastern mind, as Van Vloten claims. By prophecy here we mean guessing at the unseen and claiming to reveal the secrets of the future. We find echoes of it in ancient traditions, such as the legends of Typhon and Horus and the Persian story of Mithra. Indian and Chinese beliefs are likewise rich in stories and legends about knowing what the future holds. In Greek tradition, the prophecies of Apollo were famous, as were his priests at Delphi, who foretold the signs of things to come and claimed to know the mysteries of the future. Scandinavian folklore and the legends of Central Asia offer many more examples of belief in prophecies. Even today, people in both East and West believe in such things and promote them in books.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00254

We believe this phenomenon tells us something about the human condition: people find themselves in distress, feel powerless in the face of difficult circumstances and long for a way out. It is hardly surprising that these beliefs spread in times of disaster and severe crisis. Islam forbade belief in magic, sorcery and superstition, and condemned fortune-tellers, magicians and astrologers, “even if they happen to speak the truth”.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00255

Belief in such predictions therefore entered Islamic thought from outside it, although it had already left its mark on pre-Islamic Arab tradition. It spread among Muslims from the early days of Islam through Jews and Christians. Ibn Khaldun deals with the subject in his Muqaddima under the heading “The Nature of Prophecy, Divination, Dreams, Fortune-tellers and Other Ways of Perceiving the Unseen”. He distinguishes prophecy from divination:
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00257

The defining quality of prophecy is truth; falsehood can never enter into it. It comes from a connection made by the prophet himself with the higher realm, without an intermediary or any outside aid. The diviner, however, is not able to do this and must rely on impressions from outside himself. These impressions enter into his perception and mingle with what he is trying to perceive. His perception becomes confused by them, and falsehood finds its way in.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00258
We do not deny the prophecy of the prophets themselves. What we reject is the claim that other people can foretell the future. Ibn Khaldun, however, believed that:
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00260

Among human beings are people who, by virtue of the nature they were born with, can tell of things before they occur. These include fortune-tellers, those who gaze into transparent objects or examine the hearts and livers of animals, those who read omens in birds and wild beasts, those who cast pebbles and grains, and so forth.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00261

Ibn Khaldun was certainly influenced here by Hellenistic philosophy, particularly its ideas about the nature of the human soul and its different levels. Of particular importance was Aristotle's theory of emanation — the idea that things flow from a higher source — which had a marked influence on philosophy through the translation of Aristotle's works and through Neoplatonism.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00262

In any case, the Abbasids used prophecies in their appeals to win the hearts of the mawali. They certainly drew on ancient Persian prophecies for this purpose. Perhaps the most important prophecy the Persians believed in, and which the Abbasid organisers promoted, was that of the return of the awaited Mahdi. It acquired a distinctly Abbasid character. Among the movement's followers there was widespread talk of “the appearance of the man with the black banners, who will come from the East and bring down the throne of the Umayyads”.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00263

This was why the Abbasids adopted black banners, giving them names such as the Banner of the Shadow and the Banner of the Clouds. They interpreted the shadow and the clouds to mean that just as clouds cover the earth with their shade, and the earth is never without shade, so it will never be without an Abbasid imam. They had a third banner called the Banner of Victory, which encouraged their followers to believe that victory was inevitable.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00264

The Abbasids were also influenced by Jewish prophecies through books of malahim (predictions of momentous events) held by Jews in the Islamic world. A malhama is a momentous event that cannot fail to happen. These predictions consisted of combinations of obscure symbols that were supposed to reveal what the future held. One such prophecy spread by the organisers at the time said that “A son of A son of A will kill M son of M”. Its interpretation was that the movement founded by Ali ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Abbas would destroy the state of Marwan ibn Muhammad, the last Umayyad caliph.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00265

In short, the spread of these prophecies and the hold they had over people's minds testify to the skill of the secret Abbasid movement and the effectiveness of its psychological appeals. They captured the imagination of ordinary people and prepared them for revolution.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00266

Let us now examine the structure of the underground Abbasid organisation and how it rallied the people in the years leading up to the revolution. Its leadership clearly lay with the imam, who remained out of sight in the village of Humayma. He directed the movement, selected organisers whom he trusted and assigned their areas of activity. The organisers would come to him at set times to keep him informed of their progress. He, in turn, sent them letters containing his instructions, guidance and advice. We have found none of these letters from the years of preparation, but we have many of them from the period after the revolution's success.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00267

During those years of preparation, three men from the Abbasid family rose to prominence, none of whom would live to reap the fruits of their efforts. The first was Ali ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Abbas. He led the movement from the death of Abu Hashim ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya until 117 AH. He is credited with organising its advocates and representatives in Iraq and Khurasan. His son Muhammad then took over after his death and remained in charge until 125 AH. He was inactive and unenthusiastic, preferred to play safe and stopped corresponding with the organisers. It appears that he came under pressure from the family of Ali and was accused of seeking power for himself. This caused confusion among the organisers in Khurasan and allowed one of them, a man named Khidash, to try to turn the movement back towards the family of Ali. It was also said that he sought to build a following for himself on the basis of Persian nationalism, drawing on a revival of the old Persian religion of the Khurramiyya. Perhaps this was one reason the imam stopped writing to the organisers in Khurasan.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00268

Ibrahim ibn Muhammad then took over and performed his task well. Under his leadership, the movement reached the height of its strength, and he eventually called on its organisers to emerge from secrecy. But the Umayyad Marwan ibn Muhammad quickly had him arrested and imprisoned, then killed. By now the movement had grown strong, and it soon brought down both Marwan and the Umayyad state.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00269

The imams were assisted by a group of organisers drawn from the mawali and close associates of the Abbasid family. They therefore knew the movement's secrets and the identity of the imam of the time. They were all of a similar kind and possessed considerable military talent, were devoted heart and soul to the cause, and were adept at diplomacy, tact, dealing with changing circumstances and winning supporters. They spoke with courtesy, eloquence and skill, adapting their words to the occasion. The imams took care to prepare them especially for their task before entrusting them with the work of the movement. Their military, psychological and cultural preparation lay behind the success of their efforts. They travelled the country in the guise of merchants and scholars, spreading the movement's ideas and winning followers. They remained devoted to the cause despite the killing, crucifixion and torture they suffered. Among the best-known organisers in Iraq were Maysara al-Abdi, Bukayr ibn Mahan and Abu Salama al-Khallal, who became known as the “Minister of Muhammad's Family”.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00270
Among the most famous organisers in Khurasan were Sulayman ibn Kathir and Abu Muslim al-Khurasani, the man who was destined to proclaim the revolution and lead it to victory.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00271

The next rank in the movement consisted of the nuqaba, or representatives, who answered to the organisers. Each organiser had twelve representatives under him, chosen for their abilities and in contact only with their own organiser. Their role was to carry out the movement's plans, recruit people for the next rank down and oversee their activities. Each representative was assisted by seventy agents, who administered the underground organisation and formed its local groups among the people of the towns and villages. Van Vloten suggested that the Abbasid organisation was influenced on the one hand by the Jewish council of disciples and on the other by the council of consultation in the Prophet's time. Whatever the truth of that may be, what is certain is that the Abbasids built a tightly organised movement, bringing every psychological, military and cultural means to bear on its success.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00272

Within the first three decades of the second century AH, their cause had spread throughout most of the eastern Islamic world. There were organised groups ready and eager to support it at the first signal in the Khurasani towns of Damghan, Sarakhs, Nasa, Nishapur, Qumis, Merv, Herat, Bushanj and Abiward. Their support extended to some sixty villages in Khurasan. In these towns and villages, the movement brought together a wide range of Iranian, Arab and Turkish peoples and groups, uniting them all under the Abbasid banner.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00273

On 25 Ramadan 129 AH, Abu Muslim al-Khurasani proclaimed the revolution and raised the black banners. After a series of victories, he gained control of Khurasan. The revolutionaries then turned towards Iraq under the leadership of an Arab, Qahtaba ibn Shabib, who defeated the Umayyad armies. In Jumada al-Akhira 132 AH, the Abbasid forces led by Abd Allah ibn Ali, a member of the Abbasid family, defeated the army of Marwan ibn Muhammad at the Zab River. This was the decisive battle that brought down Umayyad rule and established the Abbasid caliphate.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00274

The underground movement had achieved its aims, and the Islamic world underwent a profound transformation. The role of the Arabs in shaping its affairs diminished. The mawali stepped onto the stage to take on that same role with skill and ability. The consequences were of enormous importance in political, economic, social and cultural life.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00275

The underground Abbasid organisation did not disappear with the success of the revolution. It was no longer confined to Iraq and Khurasan, but spread throughout all the provinces. It took on new duties and responsibilities suited to the circumstances that followed the revolution.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00276

Its original purpose had been to spread the movement's ideas and prepare for the revolution. Its duty was now to strengthen the loyalty of the Abbasid supporters to the caliphate and its policies, protect the gains won by the revolutionaries, and uncover enemies of the revolution and any plots they might be hatching. It also kept watch over the governors and officials to see that they followed state policy in their provinces. It kept the caliphs informed of shortcomings and failings in the provinces that might cause unrest among the people, and offered advice on the best ways to put things right.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00277

We learn all this and more from the letters the caliphs sent to the heads of the underground organisation in the provinces. They were known as the “Thursday Letters”. We do not know why they were given that name, but perhaps the organisers read them aloud to members of the organisation at special meetings held on Thursdays. A number of these letters survive. They were composed in the state correspondence office in the name of the caliph. Here are selected passages from a letter sent by the caliph al-Ma'mun, the Commander of the Faithful:
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00279

To those among the people of Khurasan and the other Muslims who have pledged allegiance to the truth and come to the aid of the faith ... You, people of Khurasan, have enjoyed three distinctions under the rule of the Commander of the Faithful. God has singled you out for their blessings and established their degrees of honour. The first of these distinctions is the support your forebears gave to the Prophet's family and to the last of his heirs among the forefathers of the Commander of the Faithful. The second is the support God commanded you to give him in his second call. The third is the sincerity of your hearts and the wholehearted loyalty you have shown.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00280

So, you loyal followers of the Commander of the Faithful, remind yourselves often of the favour made easy for you, of the difficulties smoothed away for you, and of the victory over those who departed from the faith and opposed the people of the Qibla [those who pray facing Mecca]. Their homes and wealth were made available to you, and through God's grace you became the guardians of the faith, the supporters of rightly guided imams and the strongholds of all Muslims.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00281

Those who bear you ill will, followers of the Commander of the Faithful, have their eyes upon you. They look at you with envy and rivalry. Some are openly hostile, others secretly flatter you, and still others have joined your ranks and mingled with your people. They feel safe among you, and it is easier for them to strike at your state through false appearances and deception, inflicting deeper wounds and greater harm. Be on your guard against such people, for it is often those who lack the strength to act openly who resort to trickery. Even a resolute man in the hour of his victory must beware of subtle deceit and hidden enticements.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00282

Let the first thing you cultivate in yourselves, and persist in cultivating, be good conduct. Be fair to one another and give those among you of virtue and honourable deeds the precedence and respect they deserve.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00283

Know that the Commander of the Faithful takes greater care over your education, your good conduct and your honourable way of life than he does over those of other people. If he considers it his duty to set his subjects on the right path and guide them towards what will help them live uprightly, then he owes even greater care to those who are closest to him and have the strongest claim on his attention. For giving priority to your moral instruction and guidance carries its own risks [the wording of this clause is uncertain].
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00284

The Commander of the Faithful asks God, who in His generosity has invited us to pray and has promised to answer us, saying, “Call on Me, and I will answer you,” to unite you in all that pleases Him, to bind you together in obedience, to let you enjoy the finest of the blessings He has bestowed upon you and inspire you with such gratitude that He will continue to give you more. May He protect you from the schemes of the unbelievers and the envy of the wrongdoers. May He preserve the Commander of the Faithful among you as He has best preserved a rightly guided imam among his friends and followers, and bear for him the weight of the responsibility he carries for you. In God the Commander of the Faithful seeks help as he strives to reward you with goodness and guide you along the best path. He is content with God as his helper and protector. God is sufficient as a protector, and God is sufficient as a helper. Peace be upon you, and God's mercy and blessings.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00285

Here are some further excerpts, this time from a letter that one of the heads of the underground organisation sent to the caliph al-Rashid. In it he pledges his loyalty, offers counsel and praises the caliph's virtues and the wisdom of his rule:
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00287

Now then, I ask God to grant the Commander of the Faithful in the years ahead the best of what He has granted him in the past: the safety with which He has guarded him against misfortune, the strength with which He has overcome his enemies, and the victory with which He has established him in the land. Through these blessings, both those already given him and those yet to come, may he be remembered for his goodness longer than any of God's other caliphs, may the marks of his justice endure the longest, may his life be the longest and may his return to God be the finest of all.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00288

We give praise to God, who has made His blessings upon the Commander of the Faithful a testimony to his standing and rank in God's sight. With these, he has no need of the testimony of those who praise him or the descriptions of those who sing his praises. God has made it a duty for His servants to speak of His blessings upon the Commander of the Faithful, to serve them faithfully and to strive against those who plot against them. He has made this a test by which to try them and distinguish one from another. Whoever among his subjects makes it his chief concern to speak of the caliph, to recount his good qualities and virtues and to acknowledge his rightful claim to obedience, has chosen the worthiest course and the one with the best outcome in this world and in his faith. Whoever changes course, whether emboldened by some power of his own or won over by a new doctrine, will find that God’s argument in favour of the Commander of the Faithful is enough to deal with him. ... Given the kinship God has granted me with him — that is, with the Commander of the Faithful — and the great duty I know I owe him for all the kindness he has shown me, I have hoped that no one who looks upon him with solicitude will be more ready than I to offer what God has made him worthy of. If I achieve what I intend, it will be through God's help. If I fall short, it will be the shortcoming of one who has done his utmost.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00289

... I wanted the Commander of the Faithful to know that in everything he has done for his subjects, he has a clear justification and a recognised defence. If someone speaks of it in the company of his closest advisers, it will be well received. If a letter explaining it is read aloud to the people, it will strengthen the case for it.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00290

Praise be to God, who has made him and his descendants the guardians of these blessings and singled them out for these virtues. We ask God to preserve him and them for the faith whose breaches He has repaired through them, for the truth whose path He has made clear through them, and for the justice whose guiding signs He has made clear through them.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00291

In conclusion, the letters exchanged between the caliphs and their organisers prove that the underground organisation continued to exist and spread throughout the provinces during the early Abbasid period, right up to the reign of al-Mutawakkil. After that, the organisation began to break apart and eventually disappeared as the Turks seized control of the affairs of the caliphate and monopolised power and influence. This was followed by the Buyid conquest of Iraq and then the Seljuk conquest. Out of these developments came the collapse of the system of the caliphate, the rise of independent states and the disintegration of the unity of the Islamic world.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00292
The Mu'tazilites
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00293
From Reason to Political Action
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00294

For all that has been written about the Mu'tazilites, parts of their history are still far from clear. Most studies deal with their ideas and beliefs; relatively few explore the part they played in politics during the closing years of Umayyad rule and throughout the Abbasid era. As a result, the subject has attracted more attention from scholars of philosophy and Islamic thought than from historians. Even those who have written the history of the Mu'tazilites have treated them as little more than a school of religious thought, unlike other schools that stood for particular religious, political and social causes. One historian writes: “The Mu'tazilites had no such organisations, nor were they separate from the Sunni community.” Scholars of philosophy, meanwhile, have studied their ideas in isolation from the social and historical conditions that gave rise to them and shaped them as they developed. We therefore need to bring together the perspectives of the historian and the student of ideas. Only then can we see the full significance of the part the Mu'tazilites played in Islamic history and civilisation.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00295

Perhaps the focus on their religious thinking is understandable: the Mu'tazilites pioneered one of the most important currents in Islamic thought, the movement that placed its trust in reason. Yet their role was no less important in politics and in the social development of the Islamic world. Admittedly, their political and social role in early Islam and under the Umayyads seems modest compared with that of the other opposition parties. This is partly because they came onto the scene later, around the beginning of the second century AH, whereas the other groups had emerged much earlier, during the great civil war. But it also had to do with the different ways they chose to fight for their cause.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00296

The Mu'tazilites put their faith in education and enlightenment. The other opposition parties resorted first to open revolutionary violence and later to organised underground rebellion. These different approaches brought different results. The Mu'tazilites gained a foothold within the government, came to dominate it and steered it towards their own aims. The struggles of the left, on the other hand, led to the founding of independent states opposed to the existing government.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00297

The deep differences between Mu'tazilite and Sunni thought, the different ways the Mu'tazilites and the parties of the left confronted the caliphate, and the moderation of some Mu'tazilite beliefs — such as the view that a Muslim guilty of a serious sin occupies a position between faith and unbelief — have led some scholars to regard the Mu'tazilites as a party of the centre, somewhere between the government and the opposition. Even if we accept this view, we must distinguish them from the Murji'ite centre, which began by justifying the government and only much later turned against it. The Mu'tazilites were enlightened liberals. At the heart of their political and social ideas lay a concern for human dignity. They hoped to put their principles into practice through education and reform rather than revolution and the overthrow of governments. Even when they turned to organised underground activity, their first aim was a revolution in culture and thought. Their second was to support the political and social opposition led by the descendants of Ali. Rarely did they seek to establish independent states founded on their own beliefs.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00298

There can be no doubt that the Mu'tazilites pioneered the use of reason in Islam. There is a close connection between a commitment to reason and opposition to conservative government claiming religious authority. That is why Mu'tazilite ideas found little favour with the Sunni caliphate, except under a few enlightened caliphs. They aroused the anger of scholars who based their teachings on transmitted accounts of the Prophet and traditionalists loyal to the caliphate. These men branded the Mu'tazilites political rebels, social anarchists and religious deviants. The Sunni scholar al-Shahrastani, for instance, called them the “Magians of the Muslim community” — a comparison with followers of the old Persian religion. Unable to find fault with their enlightened ideas or their noble aims, their enemies turned their anger against the individuals themselves. They accused them of moral corruption, debauchery, contempt for religion and an attempt to destroy Islam and replace it with pagan thought. All the evidence they put forward on these charges was taken from the slanders of a man who had broken with the Mu'tazilites, Ibn al-Rawandi, without any attempt to check or examine his claims.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00299

Sadly, the works and essays of the Mu'tazilites have been lost, leaving the writings of their enemies as a source of information about their ideas. It hardly needs saying that the leading Mu'tazilite thinkers wrote extensively on all kinds of subjects in their day. Wasil ibn Ata wrote eleven books; every one of them has been lost. Abu al-Hudhayl wrote twelve hundred treatises in answer to his opponents, and not a trace of any of them has been found. The Mu'tazilite thinker al-Nazzam wrote many essays on philosophy, the oneness of God and arguments against those who disagreed with him. All have disappeared. Al-Jahiz wrote hundreds of treatises on the same subjects, of which only a tiny fraction remains. During the persecution of the Mu'tazilites under al-Mutawakkil, the traditionalist scholars competed with one another to burn these works, hoping to draw closer to God and strike a blow at their opponents. This is why books about the different schools of Islam — particularly the works of Ash'arite and Hanbalite writers such as al-Baghdadi, al-Shahrastani, Ibn Hazm, Ibn al-Qayyim and others — are so bitterly hostile to the Mu'tazilites, presenting their ideas as a kind of paganism and heresy.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00300

It is hardly surprising that modern scholars have been influenced by this approach, whether they agree with it or react against it. Some have greatly exaggerated the influence of foreign ideas on the Mu'tazilites. Others have gone to the opposite extreme, treating their thought as a purely Islamic development. Among those who take the first view are Western scholars of the East such as Thomas Arnold, De Boer and MacDonald, who link the origins of the Mu'tazilites to Christian and Jewish theology and the heritage of ancient Greek thought. Zuhdi Jar Allah followed their lead. He traced the Mu'tazilite belief that the Quran was created to Jewish thought, and their rejection of distinct divine attributes, their willingness to interpret scripture beyond its literal meaning and their belief in free will to Christian thought. He also pointed to their use of Aristotle's logic in shaping these ideas. A modern researcher, by contrast, has tried to establish the Islamic roots of Mu'tazilite thought, arguing that the questions it dealt with had already been raised in the days of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and the first caliphs, before the Arabs had opened themselves to foreign ideas.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00301

Other scholars have taken a middle course. Becker, for example, held that the Quran was the wellspring from which the Mu'tazilites drew their basic beliefs, although Greek philosophy influenced how they expressed them. He also noted that they tackled certain fundamental philosophical questions in the manner of the Greek philosophers, such as whether motion occurs in leaps, how one action produces another, and the distinction between a thing itself and its changing qualities. In much the same vein, Ahmad Amin described Mu'tazilite thought as “a blend of both currents, Islamic and foreign”.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00302

We believe that the questions the Mu'tazilites raised are among the basic questions that arise naturally in the human mind, with no need for one culture to influence another. Indeed, most of them — questions of free choice and fate, of God and his attributes, and so on — have been asked since ancient times and are still being asked today. The Quran addresses these matters in many chapters and verses, and from a very early date Muslims offered different interpretations. The heart of the disagreement is how far we should make use of reason. Should the mind be given free rein to interpret a text and discover its deeper meaning, or must it stick to the literal meaning of the words and go no further?
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00303

The Mu'tazilites took the first path. It had been opened up in early Islam by the Qadarites, who defended human freedom of choice. The Mu'tazilites developed this approach further, drawing on other religions and ancient philosophies that shared their way of thinking. In other words, they used reason to establish the soundness of their understanding of what the Quran said about these questions. Or perhaps we might say that they “gave faith a rational foundation”, supporting, in the words of H. A. R. Gibb, “the moral philosophy derived from the Quran by drawing on Greek philosophies and the writings of Hellenistic Christian religious debate”. Thanks to the Mu'tazilites, “the Quran and Aristotle were read side by side and were sincerely regarded as complementing one another”. They succeeded in bringing “Greek thought and the Islamic religion into harmony — the oneness of God and philosophy”.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00304

There is no need to dwell at length on how the Mu'tazilites enriched Islamic thought by turning to reason whenever they faced a difficult question. Scholars agree that they laid the foundations for the reasoned study of Islamic beliefs, paved the way for Islamic philosophy and defended Islam against its critics. A few points are worth drawing attention to here.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00305

First. We owe the Mu'tazilites the recognition that reason is a source of knowledge. They challenged superstition, magic, trickery and other claims that could not stand up to rational thought, such as sightings of jinn (unseen beings) and stories of the moon splitting in two. They did not hesitate to question these legends, even when they were attributed to some of the Prophet's leading companions. In doing so, they laid the first foundations of a scientific approach to thinking.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00306

Second. Their scientific way of thinking can also be seen in the importance they placed on doubt and experiment. They looked for the causes behind things, whether in the universe, the material world, society or human life. One of their leading thinkers put it this way:
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00308

A cause may be present without producing its effect, because something can get in the way and prevent that effect from arising. But once the cause is present and all obstacles are removed, the effect must follow, just as an action inevitably follows when all the motives for it are in place.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00309

In this way, they were forerunners of the great philosophers of Islam, such as al-Kindi, al-Farabi and Ibn Sina. They also paved the way for Ibn al-Haytham and Jabir ibn Hayyan to apply the method of experiment to the study of nature.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00310

Third. At its heart, Mu'tazilite thought is constructive and life-affirming. It places great value on the individual, breaks the chains that limit freedom of thought and action, and opens new horizons for the mind to think and create. It does this by affirming our freedom to choose.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00311

The opposite belief — that everything is decided for us in advance — reduces a person to a feather in the wind. It teaches people to bow before fate, to feel powerless, to depend on others and to lose their own sense of self.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00312

Creativity and respect for individuality go hand in hand. The sciences, arts and literature of ancient Greece flourished because people valued individuality. In much the same way, the backwardness of medieval Europe was a direct result of the Catholic Church's suppression of the individual spirit.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00313

Fourth. There is a close connection between the Mu'tazilites' belief in reason and their commitment to social justice. The very people who led the way in enlightened thinking were also champions of equality. It is no wonder that they became known as the People of Justice and the Oneness of God. Al-Masudi called them the People of Justice. One modern scholar has devoted a chapter to explaining what freedom meant for the Mu'tazilites in social terms. We will test that account by looking at their political activity.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00314

Fifth. The Mu'tazilites enriched Islamic thought by giving reason a firm place within it. But they also did more to uphold and defend Islamic beliefs against their opponents than the scholars of the prophetic traditions and other traditionalists did. Followers of the older religions who were hostile to Islam sought to undermine it through secret movements or open campaigns. In the Abbasid era these became widespread, in what was known as zandaqa, or heresy. The jurists and scholars of the prophetic traditions could not defend Islam merely by quoting sacred texts when faced with opponents who argued from reason and logic. The Mu'tazilites met them on their own ground. Their debates and writings in answer to materialists, believers in rival divine powers, the Sumaniyya, the followers of Bardaisan, Jews and Christians scarcely need an introduction. Suffice it to say that many followers of other faiths embraced Islam out of conviction, thanks to the leading Mu'tazilite thinkers who defended it with reasoned arguments. In doing so, they earned Islamic thought considerable respect.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00315
Let us now look at the political activity of the Mu'tazilites in the light of their ideas and what they actually did under the Umayyads and the Abbasids.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00316

The Mu'tazilites emerged in Basra around 100 AH as a school of religious thought with beliefs of its own. Its founder was Wasil ibn Ata, who withdrew from the study circle of his teacher, al-Hasan al-Basri. His followers became known as the Wasiliyya, or the Mu'tazilites. Accounts differ as to how the latter name came about. Exploring its origins can shed a great deal of light on their political thought and social background. Al-Shahrastani traces it to something al-Hasan al-Basri said when Wasil ibn Ata left his circle: “Wasil has withdrawn from us.” On this account, he and his followers came to be called the Mu'tazilites — those who withdraw. Al-Baghdadi believes that the name arose because they departed from the consensus of the Muslim community over the status of someone who commits a grave sin. Al-Masudi, on the other hand, thought it referred to their belief that a person guilty of such a sin stood apart from both believers and unbelievers, in a position between the two. The Mu'tazilite al-Murtada held that they had given themselves the name because they rejected beliefs and innovations that had been introduced into the religion.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00317

What stands out in these differing explanations by Sunni historians of religious sects is the hostility and prejudice towards the Mu'tazilites. This makes it difficult to take them at face value. Al-Murtada's account, too, displays a pointless bias. Both approaches lean on the literal meaning of the word. It is more logical to look for the name's origins in a particular intellectual and political stance, as with the names of the other groups. The scholar Nallino believes that the word originally referred to the political stance of the Prophet's companions who remained neutral during the great civil war. The Mu'tazilites borrowed the name to express their own neutral position in the dispute between the groups over the status of a person who commits a grave sin. Nallino seems to have been influenced by an account in al-Nawbakhti:
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00319

When Uthman was killed, the people pledged allegiance to Ali, peace be upon him, and were known as the community. Later they split into three groups. One remained loyal to Ali ibn Abi Talib. Another withdrew, together with Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Abd Allah ibn Umar, Muhammad ibn Maslama and Usama ibn Zayd. These men withdrew from Ali, peace be upon him, and refused either to fight against him or to fight alongside him, even though they had pledged their allegiance to him and accepted his leadership. Thus they were called the Mu'tazilites, and became the forebears of the Mu'tazilites for all time.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00320

This view gains support from al-Subki, who says that he came across a Mu'tazilite book that began by naming Abd Allah ibn Masud as a pioneer of their movement. As we know, he was one of the Prophet's leading companions who withdrew from the fighting during the great civil war because they doubted the justice of the rival sides' claims.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00321

The political thinking of the Mu'tazilites bears the marks of enlightened moderation. Their belief that the person who commits a grave sin stands somewhere between faith and unbelief was a middle course between the extremes of the Kharijites, who declared that person an unbeliever, the leniency of the Sunnis, who regarded that person as a believer, and the Murji'ites, who evaded the issue by refusing to pass judgement at all. Wasil ibn Ata seems to have tried in his day to bring the opposition forces together, heal their divisions and unite their efforts against the Umayyad caliphate. His views on leadership bear this out. He agreed with the Kharijites that the Muslim community had the right to choose its own leader, whether from the tribe of Quraysh or from elsewhere. He also came close to the Shia position when he argued that people in every age were bound to have a leader. As we have already seen, all the opposition parties were adapting their political beliefs at that time. Their ideas drew closer together, and they came to one another's aid in their opposition to the Umayyads during the dynasty's final years.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00322

Nothing illustrates this coming together of ideas better than the fact that the Mu'tazilites drew most of their principles from the enlightened ideas circulating in Basra at the time. From the Qadarites they took the belief in free choice and in people's responsibility for their own actions. From the Jahmiyya — the followers of the Murji'ite Jahm ibn Safwan — they adopted the rejection of distinct divine attributes, the belief that the Quran was created and the view that God cannot be seen with the eyes in the life to come. This explains why some scholars have confused the Jahmiyya with the Mu'tazilites and the Qadarites. The duty to promote what is right and oppose what is wrong — one of the five basic principles of the Mu'tazilites — was among the most important beliefs of the Kharijites. The Mu'tazilites disagreed with the Shia over the doctrine that the Prophet had designated a successor and the belief that the leaders of the community were protected from error. Yet they shared many of the Shia's views on leadership, as well as their willingness to interpret the deeper meaning of sacred texts. Al-Murtada even thinks it likely that Wasil and Amr ibn Ubayd, the two leading figures in the movement, studied under Abu Hashim ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya. And despite their disagreement with al-Hasan al-Basri over the person who commits a grave sin, they agreed with him on divine justice and free choice.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00323

In short, the Mu'tazilites saw nothing wrong with building their school of thought by choosing from the wisest ideas of their time, ideas that had originally been inspired by Islam. They then gave those ideas a philosophical form, drawing on the heritage of other cultures in the process.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00324

With its five basic principles, the political and social outlook of the Mu'tazilite movement was in harmony with the demands of the mawali, who called for the Islamic law to be put into practice, with its promise of justice and equality. It is worth remembering that the leading figures of the Mu'tazilite movement were mawali who were sincere in their Muslim faith and sought to put its teachings into practice through reform and education rather than violence and revolution. Wasil ibn Ata and Amr ibn Ubayd, the founders of the movement, were renowned for their devotion and upright character. Both were mawali. Abu al-Hudhayl al-Allaf, the leading Mu'tazilite of Basra, was a client of the Abd al-Qays tribe. Ibrahim ibn Sayyar al-Nazzam, the teacher of al-Jahiz, was a Basran from among the clients of the family of Ziyad. Thumama ibn Ashras, another leading figure among the Mu'tazilites of Basra, was a client of the Banu Numayr. And al-Jahiz, the most famous Mu'tazilite scholar, a man of extraordinarily wide learning, was also one of the mawali of Basra.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00325

Because their leaders were not Arabs, because they drew deeply on the heritage of the ancient world in shaping their ideas, and because they resented the Umayyad government, they were accused of ethnic partisanship, heresy and opportunism. Yet the leaders of the Mu'tazilites fought ethnic prejudice even as they sought to give the movement for the equality of peoples — Shu'ubiyya — a truly international, Islamic meaning. In other words, they called for unity among the Muslim peoples on the basis of equality. Al-Jahiz writes:
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00327

The mawali are more like the Arabs, closer to them and more intimately bound to them, because the teachings of Islam have made them one with the Arabs. They count as Arabs in claims of kinship, in the shared responsibility of kin to pay compensation, and in matters of inheritance. If this is so, the Banawi is a man of Khurasan, and if the man of Khurasan is the client of an Arab, then the man of Khurasan, the Banawi, the client and the Arab are all one. At the very least, the things they have in common far outweigh the things that divide them. Indeed, in the most important matters, in all that really counts and in the main bonds of kinship, they agree. Once this is understood, hearts become more forgiving, the complications disappear, old grudges die out and there is no longer any reason to resent one another. All that remains is the envy and rivalry that will always exist among close relatives and neighbours.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00328

The accusation of heresy falls apart in the face of their deep devotion to Islam and their defence of it against its opponents, even when those opponents came from their own people. They were, then, “a school of thought passionately devoted to religion and determined to defend it”. Nor can their opposition to Umayyad rule be put down to personal ambition. They were known for their simple way of life and their refusal to seek favours. Despite their poverty and great need, they lived honourably, refused to stoop to dishonest ways of making a living and avoided anything that might bring their conduct into question. A modern researcher was therefore right to say of them:
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00330

The Mu'tazilite school was something like a community of educated people who judged a person's place in society by their culture and ideas. They had no faith in ethnic prejudice. Their struggle was fought in the worlds of thought and politics. What brought them together were the values of the new society and the elements that made up its civilisation, a blend of the Arab heritage and the new intellectual gains from cultures that had been introduced or revived in the lands conquered by the Muslim Arabs.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00331

The Mu'tazilites opposed the Umayyads because, in their eyes, they were tyrants who had seized the caliphate, imposed their rule by the sword and justified it with the belief that all human actions are predetermined. The Mu'tazilites, by contrast, championed freedom of choice. There is a close connection between the belief in predestination and tyranny, just as there is between the belief in human choice and freedom. That is why Muawiya is regarded as the first to teach and defend the doctrine of predestination. He “claimed that his actions were decreed and created by God, using this as an excuse for what he did, making people believe that he was in the right and that God had made him their leader and entrusted him with power”.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00332

The belief in free choice had a political meaning for the Mu'tazilites. It called on people to resist unjustly seized power, on the grounds that such power had been brought into existence by human actions and could only be brought down by human actions in return, since people are free to decide how they act. There is therefore no getting away from the fact that the Mu'tazilites rejected the rule of Muawiya and his family. Ahmad Amin, on the other hand, thought their ideas favoured Muawiya more than Ali, because the leaders of the Mu'tazilites were not persecuted under the Umayyads. But Amin himself later changed his mind, writing that “all the leading Mu'tazilite thinkers support Ali's position in the war between him and Muawiya”.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00333

Al-Khayyat confirms this: “The Mu'tazilites disown Muawiya, Amr ibn al-As and those who sided with them.” Some of their leading thinkers went so far as to accuse Muawiya of atheism and unbelief. There is no contradiction whatsoever between the Mu'tazilites' belief in the position between faith and unbelief and their refusal to recognise the Umayyad government as legitimate. In the case of someone who commits a grave sin, that middle position means that the person is guilty of wrongdoing and is neither a believer nor an unbeliever. The person's wrongdoing places them at odds with the conduct expected of believers. Someone in this position has no right to lead the Muslim community and must be removed from office, even by force. Judge Abd al-Jabbar says:
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00335
It is established by the agreement of the Prophet's companions that a leader must be removed for conduct that amounts to grave wrongdoing, since the companions did not disagree on this point.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00336

The reasons why Muawiya was unfit to lead the community were therefore plain beyond doubt; at the very least, he was guilty of wrongdoing in many respects. This judgement extended to the Umayyads in general: “There is no need for us to discuss the invalidity of the leadership of Muawiya and those who followed him, the descendants of Marwan and others.” To the early Mu'tazilite leaders, the Umayyad caliphate was a monarchy in the style of Heraclius, the Byzantine emperor. Their disgraceful conduct and their actions contrary to Islamic law made them unworthy of the caliphate.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00337

Since the Umayyads had seized the caliphate unlawfully, it was the duty of the Muslim community to struggle in keeping with the principle of promoting what is right and opposing what is wrong. Most opposition groups shared this principle. They held that the use of force was a duty in resisting injustice and establishing what was right, unlike the scholars of the prophetic traditions, who forbade armed resistance even against an unjust ruler. But the opposition parties differed in how they understood that duty. The Kharijites regarded rebellion against tyrannical rulers as necessary without hesitation or delay. Some of the Imami Shia reserved this right for the imam alone; the community could offer advice but could not take up arms. The Mu'tazilites took a position between the Kharijites and the Shia. They recognised the community's right to resist injustice by force, but with certain reservations, which they expressed in these terms: “If we are a united group and have good reason to believe that we can overcome those who oppose us, and if the rising is led by a just imam.” Such caution brought together clear thinking and careful judgement about rebellion with the justice of the cause for which it was undertaken. On this basis the Mu'tazilites excused those among the Prophet's companions, the generation that followed them and the champions of justice who had held back from opposing the Umayyads rather than throwing away their lives at the hands of the rabble of Syria. “There can be no justified rebellion unless there is good reason to expect the revolution to succeed.”
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00338

So the Mu'tazilites' reluctance to confront the Umayyads was neither cowardice nor submission. They had learned from the bitter experiences of their predecessors, the Qadarites and the followers of Ghaylan, who had risen in unfavourable circumstances and been cut down by the swords of the Umayyads.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00339

Their approach to the Umayyads and the early Abbasids therefore took two forms: an effort to influence the caliphate and guide it towards reform, or organised underground activity. They did in fact succeed in winning over some of the early Umayyad caliphs, as well as some Abbasid rulers, who adopted their views and committed themselves to reform. The Umayyad caliph Yazid ibn al-Walid ibn Abd al-Malik, for instance, believed in human free will and encouraged people to accept it. He was the first caliph to embrace the five principles of the Mu'tazilites. They backed him in his contest with al-Walid ibn Yazid until he secured the caliphate. Yazid's rise to power can be seen as a political effort by the Mu'tazilites to set things right: they supported him for his piety and upright character against a rival notorious for his debauchery. Little wonder that Yazid looked to the Mu'tazilites for guidance and tried to put Islamic law into practice. Their leaders rose to great prominence under his rule. They came to dominate the affairs of government and guide them in accordance with their principles, even advising the caliph on his choice of successors who shared his religious devotion and integrity. Wellhausen was therefore right to say that the influence of the Mu'tazilites on Yazid extended beyond religion into politics and government. Their success shows that they were true to their own understanding of the duty to promote what is right and oppose what is wrong: they supported a just and devout leader when they were sure that the conditions were favourable for success.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00340

They likewise succeeded in winning over Marwan ibn Muhammad, the last of the Umayyad caliphs. He adopted their beliefs and made a determined effort to introduce reforms. But the problems he faced were too great to overcome, and Umayyad rule came to an end in 132 AH. So the Mu'tazilites had backed two losing horses: the first died within months of becoming caliph, and the second was brought down by the Abbasid revolution. They took the same approach to the Abbasids, offering counsel and advice and seeking to influence the government, as we shall see in more detail later.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00341

The other side of their approach was organised underground activity towards the end of Umayyad rule. Like the parties of the left, they began sending their advocates to the far reaches of the Islamic world to spread their teachings. It is extremely difficult to investigate the part the Mu'tazilites played in this respect, because the books dealing with their movement have been lost, above all those written by Wasil ibn Ata. Al-Khayyat mentions a work of his known as The Book of the Movement, of which no trace has been found. We know that Wasil was the one who organised the underground movement, devised its methods and plans, and defined its aims and purposes. It seems to us that the movement as Wasil conceived it had two purposes: one religious, the other political. He sent his teachers to distant regions to spread Islam in the far reaches of India, Turkestan and North Africa. He himself played a part in this work, travelling far and wide to preach Islam. Three thousand men embraced the faith through him. One of the Mu'tazilite poets said of him:
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00343
A teacher inspired in all he sets out to do, A man of countless thoughts, a traveller of distant horizons.
The Mu'tazilites: From Reason to Political Action
passage-en-00344

The leading Mu'tazilite thinkers carried on this work both in his lifetime and after his death. Ibn Khallikan tells us that Abu al-Hudhayl al-Allaf spread Islam among large numbers of followers of the old Persian religion. The debates of the Mu'tazilites with their opponents in other Islamic schools and with the leaders of other religions leave no doubt about the part they played.
